correctness.rationale: The fixed points of A composed with binary Frobenius form a binary vector space and are exactly the idempotents. In a minimal F_q dependence of binary-independent fixed vectors, normalize one coefficient to 1. Applying the semilinear map squares all coefficients; uniqueness of the normalized relation forces them into F_2, a contradiction. Hence D<=n. For k<=n, each eligible binary k-subspace has g_k ordered bases and all these bases are F_q-frames; there are Q_{n,k}(q)/g_k such subspaces. For any one of their frames the invertible group acts transitively, so the probability of sending its squared frame back to the original is 1/Q_{n,k}(q). This gives the exact moments including k=0. Comparing to q=2 and inverting the finite unit-triangular Gaussian-binomial transform gives the specified probabilities. The n=2 and n=3 histograms reduce respectively to (2,3,1)/6 and (48,98,21,1)/168; removing zero gives 2^D-1. The frozen checker and recorded finite histograms were inspected only; the proof is not inferred from those tests.

originality.rationale: The October 25 Resultary record states the same entire law for all n and all binary extensions with the same uniform labeled measure, counting zero as well. Transpose is a bijection on the uniform sample, subtracting one converts the count to nonzero idempotents, and binary logarithm recovers D. Its exact probabilities and the frozen expression are algebraically identical; the moments are those of the same known law. The different elementary proof is not a new distribution theorem.

value.rationale: The full random idempotent law is a meaningful statistic, but its entirety is already known for this sampling measure. The frame count is a concise alternative derivation; the frozen finding claims a law and its moments, not a distinct theorem or computational capability enabled by a new method. Subtracting the zero solution, rewriting known probabilities and deriving their moments leave no independently valuable new claim as submitted.
